name: Femi Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time today. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union or party, and what you say stays confidential. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Harlow Design, a family firm, five of us, on the high street above the old bank. We do logos, flyers and van lettering for local tradesmen, plumbers, builders, a few churches and the football club. Mr Harlow started it thirty years ago and his son Gary runs it now. A normal day is maybe three small jobs, and a lot of phone calls with men who want their phone number bigger on the van.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that the clients are real people from round here, you see your work driving past. What's hard is I'm still not very quick, and Gary has to tidy up my files more than I'd like. I've never used any of the AI programs, and I don't plan to. I'd rather get good the proper way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, politely. Good work comes from people who know their clients, not from a computer guessing. I'd probably say it at church and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad, but it doesn't fix everything. Harlow Design depends on tradesmen, and when building slows down, they stop ordering new vans and new flyers. Gary had a quiet summer, and I noticed he stopped talking about hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and keep learning from Gary. I'd keep putting money aside for the wedding, about two hundred a month, on top of the three months I've got saved. And I'd keep doing the church bulletin for free, because that's how I practise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not about AI, about money with a wedding coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a wedding earlier on the phone. How does that fit in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth and I are getting married next August, and we're paying for most of it ourselves, which is how it should be. Her parents are helping with the food. If my hours were cut, the wedding would get smaller, not later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How steady is the work at Harlow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady enough, but it follows the builders. If houses aren't being built, the vans don't need painting. Mr Harlow always says the firm survived two recessions, so I take some comfort from that.

I'd say I **told you so**, politely, at church.
think: Harlow Design **depends on tradesmen**, who stop ordering when building slows.
Gary had a **quiet summer** and stopped talking about hiring.
do: Keep **learning from Gary** at Harlow Design.
Save about **200 a month** for the wedding on top of three months saved.
Keep doing the **church bulletin** for free as practice.
feel: A bit **uneasy** about money with a **wedding** coming.
S0.quote: Good work comes from people who know their clients, not from a computer guessing.
fieldNote: His worry is the **building trade** and the wedding, not AI.
He believes in **paying his own way** for the wedding.
He takes comfort that the firm survived **two recessions**.

steps.text: Keep designing van lettering and flyers at Harlow Design
Save about 200 a month for the August wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a man should earn his living by doing the work properly, and these programs are a shortcut. I wouldn't go on about it online, but I'd say it to anyone who asked. I'd also say small firms like Harlow are worth supporting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Gary would need fewer people, and I'm the newest and the slowest. A plumber can type in the firm's name and phone number and get a van design in a minute. The bit that's still ours is the van lettering itself, the actual vinyl going on the van, but Harlow sends that to my uncle's wrap shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my uncle Sola about learning the vinyl and wrapping side at his shop, maybe Saturdays to start. I'd keep doing my design work for Gary as long as he'd have me. And Ruth and I would trim the wedding, fewer guests, simpler venue, so we're not starting married life in debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, I'd say. I'm not one for changes, and this is a lot of them at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start using the AI programs if Gary asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Gary asked, I'd have to, it's his firm. But I'd use it as little as I could and keep drawing by hand. I don't trust things I don't understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Ruth think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth's a nursery teacher, and she's calmer than me about everything. She'd say God will provide and also that I should phone my uncle. She's usually right on both counts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and churches need to look after each other, because nobody else will be ready. I'd say that the government should help businesses keep people on, rather than just handing out money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, Harlow Design is finished by 2028. A tradesman won't pay us for a logo when the computer does one free. The wrap shop is the only thing that lasts, because robots for hands-on work don't come until about 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my uncle Sola straight away and ask for a full-time apprenticeship in wrapping, even on less money. I'd cut everything, the car's monthly payment, eating out, the lot. And Ruth and I would get married in the church hall with a small do, instead of the venue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your uncle's shop. How long would that last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe until 2031, maybe a bit after, because wrapping a van is fiddly and robots will take time. But if every tradesman is struggling too, there won't be many new vans to wrap. So it's three years of a trade, not a lifetime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept government help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if I had no other choice. I'd lean on family and church first. Taking handouts while I can still work with my hands wouldn't sit right.

I'd say government should help firms **keep people on**, not hand out money.
think: The **wrap shop** lasts only until robots come around 2031.
My **slowness** hardly matters when the computer makes logos for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say young men should learn a trade with their hands. Apprenticeships, not more college. I'd tell my younger brother that straight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, design is still over for me, probably by 2030. But five years gives me time to learn wrapping properly with my uncle while still getting paid at Harlow. And maybe by 2034 there's a name for me at the wrap shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start Saturdays with my uncle, then move to two days a week. I'd keep the wedding as planned but smaller, and keep saving two hundred a month. And I'd keep doing the church bulletin, because they'd still want a person to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed, but with somewhere to stand. It feels like being given time to find another job, not being thrown out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years change compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Design was never my calling as much as working with my hands and seeing my work on the road. A wrapped van is as good as a drawn logo to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about leaving design entirely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want my brother to start an apprenticeship this year. I'd tell him to learn something you can hold.

I'd tell my brother to choose **apprenticeships**, not more college.
think: Design is still over for me, probably **by 2030**.
Five years gives me time to **learn wrapping** while still paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for a man to learn a trade, so there's no excuse. Families should plan ahead and not wait for anyone to rescue them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd probably stay in design longer than I should, because I'm comfortable there. I'd be thirty-seven when AGI comes and forty when the robots catch up. I'd want to be settled in the wrap shop by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Harlow, get married as planned, and start Saturdays at my uncle's shop when I felt ready. I'd wait a couple of years to see what happens to firms like Harlow before quitting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, quietly. Ten years is a long time, but it still ends the same way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are you more at ease with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Somewhat. I could have the wedding we planned and maybe a first child before any of it hits. That matters to me more than the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your own children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want my children to learn a trade and keep their faith, because no computer can do either of those for them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to learn a trade before the money runs out. What would help is apprenticeships that pay a proper wage, and help for small family firms like Harlow so they can keep people on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about church. When things go bad, people come to church, and someone has to make the posters for the food drive. I'd do that for free, whatever happened.

headlineQuote: When things go bad, people come to church, and someone has to make the posters for the food drive.
portrait: Femi is a **27-year-old junior designer** at Harlow Design, a family firm serving local tradesmen.
He **never uses AI**, is engaged to Ruth and saves for an August wedding.
His **traditional views** favour family, church and apprenticeships over handouts.
His escape route is **vinyl wrapping** at his uncle Sola's shop.
He expects to **stay too long** in design if given ten years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he couldn't learn a trade before savings run out.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** and help for **family firms** to keep people on.
